sources.title: APOD: 2026 September 21 – Cocoon Nebula Wide Field

discussion.body: The tail is dark in this visible-light image, and those filaments hide stars in the process of formation — the long streak is a stellar nursery as much as a resemblance.
What sells the comet comparison is pure geometry: a bright knot with a lane of material trailing off it, a shape the eye already knows from somewhere else.

items.title: A nebula with a 10-light-year head and a tail nearly 100 light years long
items.body:
NASA's APOD description of the Cocoon Nebula points at a crowded starfield in Cygnus, the Swan, where the eye is drawn to the nebula itself — and then to a long trail of interstellar dust clouds to its left, which makes the whole complex look a bit like a comet.

The catalogue number is IC 5146. The bright central head spans about 10 light years, and the dark, dusty tail spans nearly 100 — so in this picture the "comet" is mostly tail, a dark streak of dust roughly ten times longer than the glowing part that gives the object its name.

sources.title: Korea Box Office: Local Comedy Remake ‘The Intern’ Leads Weekend Admissions as ‘The Odyssey’ Retains Revenue Crown

discussion.body: "Top of the box office" means nothing until you name the metric — this weekend hands you both charts at once.
And the flip needs no strange audience behaviour: admissions times average ticket price is gross, so the two rankings can disagree on the same ticket sales.

items.title: One Korean weekend, two box-office winners: admissions vs. revenue
items.body:
For the weekend of Sept. 18–20, the South Korean comedy-drama remake "The Intern" debuted at the top of the local box office by ticket admissions, according to data from KOBIS, the tracking service run by the Korean Film Council. The revenue crown went elsewhere: Christopher Nolan's holdover epic "The Odyssey" continued to lead overall weekend gross, earning more than the admissions leader.

That split isn't a contradiction. Admissions count bodies through the door; gross multiplies those bodies by what each ticket cost, so a film that sells fewer tickets at higher prices can still out-earn the one that sold the most seats. Both headlines are defensible, and they are answers to different questions.

sources.title: Javier Bardem And Penélope Cruz Discuss The Hot-Button Issues Raised By Florian Zeller’s Intimate Drama ‘Bunker’ – TIFF Studio

discussion.body: The interesting choice is that it's paid work rather than a conviction — he takes a lucrative job building someone else's survivalist bunker, which makes this as much a story about a marriage's veto power as about doomsday.
Or the marriage is only the lens. The subject could be the career itself: an architect spending his talent on a rich man's bunker while his wife watches.

items.title: Zeller's 'Bunker': a paid commission becomes a marriage test
items.body:
Florian Zeller's "Bunker" casts Javier Bardem and Penélope Cruz as Miguel and Sofia, a couple living in London where Miguel's career as an architect has made him successful. The flashpoint, as Deadline reports the logline, is a job: against Sofia's wishes, Miguel accepts a lucrative offer to build a tech billionaire's survivalist bunker, a decision that tests the couple's long-term relationship.

There is a tidy irony in the setup. The man who designs buildings for a living is offered work building a shelter from the world, and the person he lives with is the one who objects. Whether Zeller treats the bunker as a symbol or merely as an expensive marital irritant is the film's business, not the logline's.

sources.title: Jann Arden headlines Calgary concert for Canadian unity ahead of Alberta referendum

items.title: Jann Arden headlines a Calgary unity concert a month before Alberta's separation vote
items.body:
A free outdoor concert headlined by Jann Arden brought thousands to downtown Calgary on Sunday, staged in support of Canadian unity — about a month before Albertans cast ballots on the question of separation.

The timing is the story: a mass gathering in Alberta, organized around the country staying together, landing in the final stretch before a vote that asks whether it should. A concert doesn't decide a referendum, but thousands turning out for a free Sunday show is a visible, countable thing.

sources.title: Winnipeg vendor in 'disbelief' after $70,000 worth of Pokemon cards stolen

items.title: A Winnipeg flea-market stall lost $70,000 in Pokémon cards in one night
items.body: A Pokémon collector is in disbelief after $70,000 worth of product and cards were stolen from his shop at a flea market in Winnipeg's South Osborne neighbourhood on Friday night. The setting is what makes the loss strange to picture: not a vault or a warehouse, but a stall, emptied of merchandise whose value sits entirely in printed cardboard — light, portable and quick to move. A shop's inventory can be worth a down payment and still fit in a car trunk.

items.title: Austin's mayor wants an independent investigation into an ICE shooting
items.body: An ICE agent shot and wounded a man in Austin, Texas. The city's mayor has called for an independent investigation into the shooting.

sources.title: Tatiana Huezo, Juan Sebastián Mesa, Mónica Lima, Val Jashari Among 10 Filmmakers Vying for WIP LatAm and Europa Awards at San Sebastián

items.title: What a 'work in progress' award at a film festival is for
items.body: San Sebastián's WIP competition showcases take in ten projects this year, selected from hundreds of submissions. Six of those are competing for the WIP Latam Industry Award. The films are, by definition, not finished — that is what a work-in-progress section means — and the festival frames the awards as a way to help the winning projects jump their last hurdles towards release. So the prize is less a verdict on a completed work than a push on a work still in the shop: industry attention delivered at the moment a film can still use it.

sources.title: Converse apologizes and pulls sneaker ad that critics said included racist imagery

discussion.body: Reading an image this closely isn't an overreaction; it's what images are for. If a triangle of light reads as a hood to a lot of people, it reads as a hood.
The reading is still a reading. The same shape is a triangle to someone who doesn't bring the association — the criticism says more about shared visual vocabulary than about the picture itself.

items.title: An ad's lighting, a skirt, and what critics saw in it
items.body: Criticism of a sneaker ad featuring K-pop singer Karina turned on two specific visual readings. Critics said a white triangular image created by lighting on her skirt resembled a KKK hood, and that the way she held the sneakers made them look like the dangling feet of a lynching victim. Whatever the intent behind the images, both complaints hinge on composition: where light falls, how a body is posed, what a shape resembles once it is isolated from everything around it. Advertisements are built to be read fast, and a reading can travel faster than the campaign.

sources.title: Ke Huy Quan Reveals “Life Changing” Gesture From Spielberg & Lucas When He Was A Kid

items.title: Ke Huy Quan Only Learned Later How Lucas and Spielberg Looked After Him
items.body: Ke Huy Quan was 12 years old when he made Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom. In his new memoir, Never Say Die, excerpted in Entertainment Weekly, he writes that producer George Lucas and director Steven Spielberg took care of him in a way he didn't know about until after filming had concluded. [...] The delay is the interesting part. A 12-year-old may not register arrangements made on his behalf, which is arguably what makes them work — and why it can take decades, and a book, to find out they existed.

sources.title: 18 suspects accused in the 2021 killing of Haiti's president being extradited from Haiti to U.S.

discussion.body: A former anti-corruption official among the accused is the detail that makes this hard to file under one heading. The people a state recruits for its own internal policing and the people later accused over a president's death turn out to be drawn from the same small pool.
Awaiting trial is not guilt. A list of suspects tells you who was arrested and held, not who is responsible — and the more varied the group, the more the prosecution has to prove separately.

items.title: Colombian Soldiers and an Ex-Anti-Corruption Official Among Those Awaiting Trial in Haiti
items.body: PBS NewsHour reports that the suspects who remain in Haiti awaiting trial over the 2021 killing of Haiti's president include more than a dozen Colombian soldiers, a former Haitian police officer and Joseph Badio, a former employee of Haiti's Ministry of Justice who was part of an anti-corruption unit. The mix is the notable thing: foreign ex-soldiers, a former police officer and a one-time internal corruption watchdog, all facing proceedings in the same case. That kind of roster resists a tidy summary — it is not obviously a coup, a contract job or a purely domestic plot, and the trial is the place where the shape of it would have to be argued rather than assumed.

sources.title: Sister of Pakistan's ex-PM Imran Khan arrested

items.title: Imran Khan's Sister Arrested, Accused of Mobilising His Supporters
items.body: BBC World reports that Aleema Khanum, the sister of Pakistan's former prime minister Imran Khan, has been arrested. She is accused of mobilising her brother's supporters ahead of country-wide protests. The allegation is about organising rather than violence, which puts the arrest in the crowded space between politics and policing. Whether the accusation holds is a question for a court; the timing, ahead of planned demonstrations, is the part supporters and critics will read very differently.

sources.title: UK should 'team up' with Canada in new Europe alliance, Canadian minister tells BBC

items.title: An EU Door Opened for Canada — as an 'Associate Member'
items.body: The president of the European Commission has proposed 'opening the door' for Canada to become an associate member of the European Union, BBC Business reports. Note the verb: this is an offer of a door, not a membership. Associate status for a country on another continent is an unusual thing to dangle, and what it would actually deliver — market access, defence coordination, a diplomatic signal — is the part that would have to be negotiated rather than announced.

sources.title: ‘Lanterns’ Review: Episode 6 Embraces ‘Bad Optics’ with a Clever Revival — Spoilers

discussion.body: The interesting part isn't the time jump; it's the missing ring. Take away the power and a Green Lantern episode has to work as an investigation — knocking on doors instead of willing problems out of existence.

Or it just underlines that the ring was the fun part. A ring-less hero returning home to dig into a death is the genre's standard move for signalling seriousness, and seriousness is not the same thing as a good case.

items.title: 'Lanterns' Takes Away the Ring and Sends John Stewart Home
items.body: The story shifts to 2026 for this episode, and it shifts with a Green Lantern who no longer has a ring. John Stewart returns to Rushville to investigate Hal Jordan's death — and, in the same trip, to find some closure of his own. That's spoiler territory, so consider this the warning before the rest of the season catches up with you.

sources.title: ‘The Other Bennet Sister’ Fans, Rejoice! Dónal Finn Will Be Back for Three-Part Christmas Special

items.title: Mary Bennet's Husband Comes Back for the Christmas Special
items.body: Dónal Finn is returning as Tom Hayward — Mary Bennet's beloved husband — for the three-part Christmas special of 'The Other Bennet Sister.' IndieWire's announcement also flags that his rival is back, which is the sort of casting detail that keeps a festive reunion from being purely festive. A husband, a rival, and tinsel: the special arrives with its tension already cast.

sources.title: The capture of Western Yemen is making the country's humanitarian crisis worse

items.title: Families in Yemen Are Being Displaced Into Areas With Too Little Aid
items.body: People in Yemen and aid groups tell NPR that the fighting is displacing families into areas without enough aid to support them. That's the part worth holding onto: displacement into under-served ground doesn't end a family's emergency, it moves it somewhere the response is thinner.

sources.title: Canada, France pledge to work together on space infrastructure, business

items.title: Canada and France Plan Shared Satellite-Ground Infrastructure
items.body:
The Prime Minister's Office says Canada and France intend to work together on infrastructure capable of receiving data from satellites — a signal that the two countries see ground segment, not just launch capacity, as the cooperative ground.

That framing matters: satellites are only useful if someone can downlink what they collect, which is why receiving stations and data-handling agreements are often the practical bottleneck in space partnerships. The announcement positions the arrangement as an infrastructure-and-business matter rather than a single mission.

What specific facilities, funding split or timeline the two governments have in mind is not part of what the PMO spokesperson described.

sources.title: Rising use of AI in Canadian courtrooms creates divide

items.title: Rising AI Use in Canadian Courtrooms Divides Experts
items.body:
Canadian courts are seeing increased use of artificial intelligence, and experts describe the result as a divide over both access to justice and the value of the work experience it creates for law students, Global News Canada reports.

Those two concerns pull in opposite directions. If AI tools lower the cost of routine legal work, more people might get help they currently cannot afford. If the same tools absorb the tasks that once trained junior lawyers and students, the pipeline that produces competent counsel narrows.

The report attributes the divide to experts; it does not settle how courts are resolving it.
